title: Domain Policy Defined Only in Persistence Queries
pattern: A core business definition or decision (e.g., who qualifies as an "active account" or a "high-value customer") is embedded solely in SQL, a database view, or a repository/query filter rather than having an explicit domain-owned definition.
why_bad: Policy hidden among persistence details is difficult to locate, discuss with domain experts, test independently, and change consistently; SQL strings are rarely checked by the compiler. Separate copies of the same business definition can drift, and entities degrade into mere data containers.
detection: Inspect SQL literals, views, and query builders for business-state criteria, thresholds, or calculations that define domain concepts such as active accounts or high-value customers. Confirm that these predicates embody policy rather than mechanical retrieval or indexing, and that the domain has no authoritative definition of the same concept.
counterexample: Primary-key or identity lookups and simple status indexing are mechanical retrieval, not domain policy. Efficient database filtering or aggregation is legitimate when it faithfully implements a domain-owned definition; loading every record to evaluate it in memory can be substantially worse.
source: *Eric Evans - Domain-Driven Design, Chapter 6, Section "REPOSITORIES"*; Scott Wlaschin, *Domain Modeling made Functional* (2017), Chapter 10, "Persistence Ignorance", p. 211, 471.
